\title{Counter-Examples Decide Whether Retraining Works, Location Decides How Fast: Repairing a Planted Shortcut in
GPT-2}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Sonu Akash, Sidhant Holla, Siddhant Khurdiya, Piyush Shiv}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Computer Science and Engineering (AI \& ML)\\
PES University, Bengaluru, India}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Interpretability tools can show where a behaviour happens inside a language model, but does that location tell us
where to repair it? We plant a shortcut with known ground truth: GPT-2 small learns IMDB sentiment while an invented
actor name always comes with the same label. The logit lens, block swaps and activation patching agree that the name
reaches the answer only in the last three blocks. Whether retraining removes
the shortcut is decided by the repair data, not the block: one epoch on clean data removes it from any single block,
because the clean data shows each name with both labels, and without these counter-examples no block removes more
than \ccNoNamesMaxFullFT{} of it. Location instead sets the speed and mechanism of repair: block~0 and the late blocks repair
fastest and blocks 1--5 slowest, a pattern we noticed after the results and then confirmed under full fine-tuning in a
test registered in advance on two new models. The tools find only the late blocks; block~0, which they miss, blocks the
trigger at the name tokens. A training-free read-out from layer~9 removes \pSixBEqLNineRemovedFullFTRange{} of the
shortcut, more than from any other layer. Under LoRA rank~64 the counter-examples are again required and block~0 is
again among the fastest blocks; memorized wrong labels, with no shared cue, can be removed by one block only.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
shortcut learning, interpretability, logit lens, activation patching, model repair, early exit, GPT-2
\end{IEEEkeywords}
